Chinese artificial intelligence firms have been leveraging the outputs of American frontier models developed by OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC to train their own AI systems for defense applications.
Chinese institutions linked to the military have been harvesting the outputs of U.S. AI models to bypass Washington’s export controls on advanced chips.
Chinese researchers are increasingly hijacking the work of America’s best-known AI startups to build advanced systems that power military applications.
Chinese researchers are misusing a technique known as model distillation, which involves using outputs and data from powerful teacher models to train smaller student models.
Through model distillation, China has developed models matching the performance of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s frontier models using far less computational resources.
Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. launched a preview of Qwen3.8, which benchmarks second only to Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and surpasses OpenAI’s GPT-5.6.
The Chinese startup Moonshot AI released the world’s largest open-weights model called Kimi K3 with claimed frontier-level performance.
U.S. officials and AI startups have accused Chinese firms of distilling American models to advance the capabilities of their own AI systems.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions on any Chinese AI firms deemed guilty of the distillation practice.
Microsoft Corp. Chief Executive Satya Nadella highlighted the irony of accusations against China, noting Anthropic’s own models were trained on massive internet data without permission.
PLA Unit 96941, the main cyberwarfare group in the People’s Liberation Army, distilled OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process and summarize sensitive military source code.
PLA Unit 96941 developed a lightweight model specializing in safely processing sensitive data on Chinese military networks from distillation of GPT-3.5 outputs.
Researchers at the North University of China used Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku to create synthetic training data to build a text classification system for social media monitoring.

Researchers at the National University of Defense Technology distilled a U.S.-made image processing model to install it on unmanned aerial vehicles for real-time video analysis aiding navigation and weapons targeting.
The White House is concerned that model distillation undermines its export controls and infringes on the intellectual property rights of U.S. model makers.
Beijing accuses the Americans of pursuing AI hegemonism regarding AI governance and safety talks.

SapienX Inc. co-founder Trevor Koverko stated that Chinese model distillation is best understood as transferring selected capabilities into cheaper, locally controlled systems and does not imply independence from frontier AI.
Chinese researchers can devise systems matching U.S. models in narrow applications but still need original breakthroughs to outperform U.S. rivals.
